newsitem.title: JAPAN: Major Japan firms seen granting higher wage rises.
newsitem.headline: Major Japan firms seen granting higher wage rises.

text.p: Japanese firms in key sectors such as cars and electronics are due to announce proposed annual salary increases for their staff on Tuesday, with many expected to grant slightly higher rises than last year.

Management and union representatives on Monday declined to comment on the planned wage rises for the fiscal year starting in April, which economists and the Japanese media say are likely to be marginally better than last year.
Firms in the car, electronics, shipping and steel industries are due to announce the wage rises on Tuesday as part of Japan's traditional "shunto" spring wage negotiations.

The rises, in response to requests from unions belonging to the Japan Council of Metal Workers' Unions (IMF-JC), are likely to have a big influence on other industries in the "shunto" or "spring offensive" wage talks.
Japanese media reports on Monday said Toyota Motor Corp had agreed to raise average monthly wages for 1997/98 by 9,400 yen, up 700 yen or 2.83 percent from the 1996/97 rise.

On bonuses, Toyota accepted the labour union's request to pay an amount equivalent to 6.1 months' basic wages, or an average of 2.08 million yen, compared to 5.8 months last year, the media reports said.

Kyodo news agency reported over the weekend, quoting industry sources, that labour and management in the electronics industry had agreed on an average 3.17 percent wage rise for 1997/98, 0.03 point higher than last year's increase.

After negotiations among Japan's 17 major electronics makers, the industry settled on a monthly rise of an average 9,027 yen for a worker aged 35, a rise of 200 yen over last year's increase, it said. It is the second straight year that the wage rise has exceeded that of the preceding year, it said.
Officials at the electronics industry's labour union and Toyota declined to comment on the reports.
Under a system introduced 40 years ago, labour representatives and management engage in shunto talks in February and March to seek unified wage increases through collective negotiation.

This year, labour is calling for increased wages because of a planned rise in the nation's sales tax to five percent from three percent in April, but their bargaining power is regarded as limited, given the weakness of the economy. --Miki Shimogori/Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-9404
